lessons.title: Randomized QuickSort
lessons.objective: Implement randomised QuickSort and prove O(n log n) expected time using the harmonic series argument for expected comparisons.
concepts: QuickSort: divide-and-conquer sort using a pivot
Deterministic pivot: O(n^2) worst case on sorted/adversarial input
Random pivot: makes worst-case O(n^2) have probability 1/n! (negligible)
Expected comparisons proof: harmonic series argument
E[comparisons] = 2n * H_n ≈ 2n * ln(n) = O(n log n)
Indicator random variable: X_{ij} = 1 if elements i and j are compared
P(i and j compared) = 2 / (j - i + 1) for sorted positions i < j
Tail probability: P(runtime > c * n log n) decreases exponentially in c
lessons.explanation: Randomised QuickSort selects the pivot uniformly at random from the current subarray. The deterministic QuickSort with fixed pivot (e.g., always last element) degrades to O(n²) on sorted input. Random pivot makes this extremely unlikely. Expected complexity proof: number the elements by their sorted rank 1 to n. Define indicator variable X_{ij} = 1 if elements with ranks i and j are directly compared during the sort. Elements i and j are compared if and only if one of them is chosen as the pivot before any element between them (in sorted order). The probability that i or j is the first pivot chosen among {i, i+1, ..., j} is 2/(j-i+1). The expected total comparisons: E[total] = sum over all pairs (i,j) of P(X_{ij}=1) = sum_{i<j} 2/(j-i+1) = 2 * sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (n-k)/(k+1) ≈ 2n * H_n ≈ 2n ln n = O(n log n). The harmonic series H_n = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n ≈ ln n. Tail bound: with high probability (1 - 1/n^c), randomised QuickSort runs in O(n log n).
lessons.analogy: Randomised QuickSort's O(n log n) proof is like proving that a fair coin game rarely produces extreme outcomes. Each comparison between elements i and j is like a coin flip: element i is compared to j only if it 'wins' the lottery of being chosen as a pivot first among all elements between them. The expected number of such wins across all pairs gives the harmonic series O(n log n) bound.

code_example.explanation: Three-way partitioning (Dutch National Flag) handles duplicate elements efficiently. When many elements equal the pivot, standard two-way partition places them on one side, causing O(n²) performance on arrays with all identical elements. Three-way partition puts equal elements in the middle, reducing them to a single group that is never recursed into.

common_mistakes: Not using random pivot when implementing QuickSort — fixed-pivot QuickSort is O(n²) on sorted or reverse-sorted arrays, which are common inputs in interviews; always randomise the pivot

Confusing QuickSort (sorting) with QuickSelect (selection) — QuickSort recursively sorts both halves; QuickSelect only recurses into the half containing the target element, giving O(n) expected instead of O(n log n)
Not using three-way partition for arrays with many duplicates — [5,5,5,5,5] sorted with standard two-way partition gives O(n²) partitions; three-way partition reduces to O(n) for all-equal arrays
lessons.interview_relevance: Randomised QuickSort analysis with the harmonic series proof appears at research-focused companies and L6+ interviews testing algorithm theory depth. The practical relevance is high: every production sort (JavaScript V8's TimSort, Java's DualPivotQuicksort) uses randomisation or careful pivot selection to avoid worst-case. The three-way partition optimisation for duplicates appears in Sort Colors (LeetCode #75, Dutch National Flag problem).
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement randomQuickSort and quickSort3Way. Run countComparisons(1000) and verify the average is close to the theoretical 2n*ln(n) ≈ 13,800 comparisons. Then implement Dutch National Flag (LeetCode #75): sort array of 0s, 1s, 2s in-place. Verify it handles [2,0,2,1,1,0] -> [0,0,1,1,2,2]. Why is the three-way partition O(n) instead of O(n log n) for this input?

flashcards.front: Randomised quicksort: how does randomisation fix worst-case O(n²)?
flashcards.back: Choose a RANDOM pivot instead of always using the first/last element. Sorted or reverse-sorted arrays (which trigger O(n²) for deterministic quicksort) become random inputs after random pivot selection. Expected O(n log n) on ANY input — adversary cannot construct a worst case.

flashcards.front: Expected comparisons in randomised quicksort: proof sketch?
flashcards.back: Elements i and j are compared iff one of them is chosen as the first pivot in the range [i..j]. Probability: 2/(j-i+1). Sum over all pairs: Σᵢ Σⱼ>ᵢ 2/(j-i+1) = 2n Hₙ ≈ 2n ln n. Total expected comparisons = O(n log n).

flashcards.front: Quicksort pivot strategies compared?
flashcards.back: ALWAYS first/last: O(n²) for sorted input. MEDIAN-OF-THREE: better in practice, still O(n²) worst case with adversarial input. RANDOM: O(n log n) expected, adversary cannot force worst case. MEDIAN-OF-MEDIANS: O(n log n) guaranteed but larger constant.

flashcards.front: Randomised quicksort: does it have O(n log n) worst case?
flashcards.back: NO — O(n²) worst case still exists (extremely unlikely but possible: always picking the minimum/maximum). However, the probability of O(n²) on any input is at most 1/n^k for any constant k → 'with high probability' O(n log n). In practice: treated as O(n log n).

flashcards.front: Introsort: how does it combine strategies?
flashcards.back: Starts with randomised quicksort. Switches to HEAPSORT if recursion depth exceeds 2×log n (indicating bad pivot choices). Fallback ensures O(n log n) worst case. Used in C++ std::sort and most production sorting implementations.

flashcards.front: Tail call optimisation in quicksort: which recursive call to optimise?
flashcards.back: Always recurse on the SMALLER partition first. This bounds the call stack depth to O(log n) (not O(n)). The larger partition can be handled iteratively (via explicit stack or tail call). Without this: O(n) stack depth on unbalanced splits.

quiz.question: Randomised quicksort on arr=[1,2,3,4,5] (sorted). Expected runtime?
options: O(n²) — sorted is worst case
O(n log n) — randomisation eliminates sorted-input pathology
O(n) — linear scan
O(n²) for first run, O(n log n) amortised
quiz.explanation: Randomised quicksort: random pivot selection means sorted order has no effect. Expected O(n log n) on any input, including sorted. The adversary cannot construct a worst case if the pivot is chosen uniformly at random.

quiz.question: Probability that elements 2 and 8 are compared in randomised quicksort on [1..10]?
quiz.explanation: Elements at positions i=2 and j=8 are compared iff one is the first pivot chosen in [2..8] (7 elements). Probability = 2/(j-i+1) = 2/7. This is the key formula for the expected comparisons proof.

quiz.question: Introsort switches from quicksort to heapsort when?
options: Array is sorted
Recursion depth exceeds 2×log₂(n) — indicating consistently bad pivots
Partition size drops below 10
First partition has size > n/2
quiz.explanation: Introsort: tracks recursion depth. If depth > 2×log₂(n): bad pivot luck is causing degenerate behaviour → switch to heapsort (O(n log n) guaranteed). Also switches to insertion sort for small subarrays (size ≤ 16). This guarantees O(n log n) worst case.

quiz.question: Randomised quicksort vs merge sort: which uses O(1) extra space?
options: Merge sort — only reads, doesn't modify
Quicksort — in-place partition (O(log n) stack only)
Both use O(n) space
Neither — both use O(n) space for the merge/partition step
quiz.explanation: In-place quicksort: partitions the array in-place using two pointers. O(log n) stack space for recursion. Merge sort: needs O(n) auxiliary space for the merge step. For memory-constrained environments: quicksort is preferred. For stable sort or guaranteed worst case: merge sort.

theory_mcq.question: The harmonic series proof shows E[comparisons] = 2n*H_n ≈ 2n*ln(n). What does the INDICATOR RANDOM VARIABLE `X_ij` represent and why does it simplify the proof?
options: X_ij represents whether elements i and j are in the same partition

X_ij = 1 IF elements i and j (at SORTED positions i<j) are DIRECTLY COMPARED at some point during the algorithm, 0 otherwise; LINEARITY OF EXPECTATION lets us write E[total comparisons] = SUM over all pairs (i,j) of E[X_ij] = SUM of P(X_ij=1); this DECOMPOSES a complex question ('how many comparisons total?') into N² SIMPLE questions ('what's the probability THIS specific pair is compared?'); crucially, linearity of expectation holds REGARDLESS of dependence between the X_ij variables, making the proof tractable even though comparisons are NOT independent events
X_ij represents the number of times the pivot is selected
X_ij is the indicator for whether the array is already sorted
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Indicator random variable: X_{ij} = 1 if elements i and j are compared' — the power of indicator variables combined with linearity of expectation: E[ΣX_ij] = ΣE[X_ij] holds even when the X_ij are dependent (which they are, since QuickSort's recursive structure correlates comparisons); this lets the proof avoid analyzing complex joint distributions.

theory_mcq.question: The claim `P(i and j compared) = 2/(j-i+1)` for sorted positions i<j. What GEOMETRIC INSIGHT explains this formula?
options: The probability is always 2/n regardless of position, and this formula is an approximation

ELEMENTS i AND j ARE COMPARED IFF one of them is chosen as PIVOT BEFORE any element strictly between them (in sorted order) is chosen; consider the SET of elements {i, i+1, ..., j} (size j-i+1); until one of these j-i+1 elements becomes a pivot, they all remain in the SAME partition (could still be compared together); among this set, i and j are compared EXACTLY WHEN the FIRST pivot chosen from this set is i OR j (not anything strictly between); since pivots are chosen UNIFORMLY at random from the current partition, P(first pivot from this set is i or j) = 2/(j-i+1) — 2 favorable outcomes out of (j-i+1) equally likely elements
The formula comes from the number of recursive calls needed to separate i and j
2/(j-i+1) represents the probability that i and j end up in the same final sorted position
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'P(i and j compared) = 2/(j-i+1) for sorted positions i<j' — this is the KEY LEMMA: i and j are compared exactly when one of them is the FIRST pivot chosen among the set {i,...,j}; since all j-i+1 elements in this range are equally likely to be the first pivot chosen (uniform random pivot), and exactly 2 of them (i or j) result in a comparison, the probability is 2/(j-i+1).

logic_mcq.question: For `randomQuickSort([3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6,5,3,5])`, the result is `[1,1,2,3,3,4,5,5,5,6,9]`. How does the algorithm handle DUPLICATE values (three 5's, two 3's, two 1's)?
options: The Lomuto partition's `<=` comparison correctly groups equal elements: when arr[i]<=pivot, the element moves to the 'less than or equal' side; this means duplicates of the pivot value end up adjacent to the pivot in the final sorted output; the algorithm correctly sorts despite duplicates because <= (not strict <) is the partition condition — confirmed by the fully sorted output containing all original elements including duplicates
Duplicate values cause infinite recursion which the algorithm avoids via a special check
The algorithm removes duplicates before sorting, then re-inserts them at the end
Duplicates are handled by treating them as a single combined element
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: randomQuickSort([3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6,5,3,5]) = [1,1,2,3,3,4,5,5,5,6,9]; the Lomuto partition's `arr[i]<=pivot` condition correctly includes pivot-equal elements on the 'left' side; this is standard correctness for duplicate handling in 2-way partition QuickSort (though it can degrade to O(n²) with many duplicates of the SAME value, motivating 3-way partition for that case).

logic_mcq.question: Why does `quickSort3Way` (Dutch National Flag) perform BETTER than 2-way partition when there are MANY DUPLICATE values?
options: 3-way partition uses a different sorting algorithm entirely for duplicates

3-WAY PARTITION creates THREE regions: [<pivot], [==pivot], [>pivot]; all elements EQUAL to the pivot are GROUPED TOGETHER and EXCLUDED from further recursion (`quickSort3Way(arr,lo,lt-1); quickSort3Way(arr,gt+1,hi)` skips the middle '==pivot' section entirely); for an array with MANY duplicates (e.g., all elements equal), 2-WAY partition would recursively process O(n) sub-arrays of decreasing size (O(n²) total), while 3-WAY partition handles all duplicates in ONE pass (O(n) total) since they never need re-partitioning
3-way partition uses a fixed pivot instead of random selection
3-way partition is always slower but more memory-efficient
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's comment: 'THREE-WAY PARTITION (Dutch National Flag) — better for many duplicates' — the key optimization: equal-to-pivot elements are isolated in the middle section [lt..gt] and EXCLUDED from recursive calls; for an array of all-identical elements, 2-way partition degrades to O(n²) (each pivot only excludes itself), while 3-way partition achieves O(n) (all duplicates handled in the first pass).

syntax_mcq.question: In `countComparisons`, the theoretical estimate uses `2*n*Math.log(n)`. Why is `Math.log` (natural log, base e) used rather than `Math.log2`?
options: Math.log2 would give a different (incorrect) asymptotic growth rate

The proof states E[comparisons] ≈ 2n*ln(n) using NATURAL LOG (the harmonic number H_n ≈ ln(n) is a standard approximation using the natural logarithm, derived from the integral approximation ∫(1/x)dx); converting to a different log BASE only changes the CONSTANT FACTOR (log2(n) = ln(n)/ln(2) ≈ 1.443*ln(n)), not the asymptotic O(n log n) growth rate; since the formula 2n*ln(n) comes directly from the harmonic series approximation (which is naturally expressed in base e), using Math.log (natural log) matches the mathematical derivation exactly, while Math.log2 would require an extra conversion factor
Math.log is faster to compute than Math.log2 in JavaScript
Natural log is required because JavaScript doesn't support Math.log2 for large n
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'E[comparisons] = 2n * H_n ≈ 2n * ln(n) = O(n log n)' — the harmonic number approximation H_n ≈ ln(n) + γ (Euler-Mascheroni constant) is naturally expressed via the natural logarithm from calculus (the integral of 1/x); the formula directly uses ln(n), so Math.log (JavaScript's natural log) is the correct, derivation-consistent choice.

lessons.title: Skip Lists
lessons.objective: Explain the skip list structure as a randomised balanced BST alternative, understand why O(log n) expected height arises from coin-flip level promotion, and implement search and insert.
concepts: Skip list: multiple levels of linked lists with random node promotion
Level 0: complete sorted linked list (all elements)
Level k: subset of level k-1 elements promoted with probability 1/2
Expected height: O(log n) levels due to geometric distribution
Search: start at top level, move right until overshoot, drop down
Insert: find insertion position, flip coins to determine height
O(log n) expected search and insert: O(log n) levels * O(1) per level
Advantages over BST: simpler concurrent implementation, no rotation logic
lessons.explanation: A skip list is a probabilistic data structure that achieves O(log n) expected search, insert, and delete without the complex rotations of balanced BSTs. Structure: Level 0 contains all elements in sorted order as a linked list. Level 1 contains every element that was 'promoted' with probability 1/2. Level 2 contains elements promoted from Level 1 with probability 1/2, and so on. The maximum level is O(log n) with high probability. Search: start at the highest level and the leftmost header node. Move right as long as the next node's key is <= the target. When stuck, drop to the next level and repeat. This is like a highway system: express lanes (high levels) cover large gaps quickly, local lanes (low levels) find the exact position. Insert: find the insertion position at each level. Then flip coins to determine how many levels the new node should appear in. O(log n) expected height because each successive level halves the expected number of nodes. Redis sorted sets (ZSET) are implemented as skip lists.
lessons.analogy: A skip list is like a train system with express and local trains on parallel tracks. The express train (high level) skips most stations, letting you travel far quickly. The local train (level 0) stops at every station. When searching, you ride the fastest train that does not overshoot your destination, then switch to progressively slower trains for the final approach. Promotion is random: each new station is 'invited' to join express trains by coin flip.

code_example.explanation: The update array in insert tracks the last node at each level that is to the left of the insertion point. This allows efficient pointer rewiring when the new node is inserted at each level. Without update, we would need to re-traverse from the top for each level of the new node.

common_mistakes: Using a fixed level instead of random level promotion — a fixed level for every node gives O(n) worst-case search; the random promotion is what gives O(log n) expected height and search time
Not initialising update[] with the header node — if no node exists at high levels, update[i] should point to the header; without this, high-level pointer rewiring would fail on the first insert
Confusing forward[i] (next node at level i) with next pointer in a regular linked list — each skip list node has an array of forward pointers, one per level it participates in
lessons.interview_relevance: Skip lists appear in system design interviews as the backing data structure for Redis sorted sets (ZSET). Understanding why Redis chose skip lists over balanced BSTs (simpler concurrent access, no rotation, O(log n) expected) is a senior-level signal. The Design a Skip List (LeetCode #1206) problem directly tests implementation.

flashcards.front: Skip list: structure?
flashcards.back: Multiple levels of sorted linked lists. Level 0: complete sorted list (all elements). Level 1: ~50% of elements (randomly promoted). Level k: ~(1/2)^k fraction of elements. Each node has a tower of pointers — one per level it participates in. Search starts at the highest level.

flashcards.front: Skip list search: algorithm?
flashcards.back: Start at highest level, head node. While target not found: if next node > target, drop down one level. If next node ≤ target, advance right. At level 0: found or not present. Expected O(log n) — drops O(log n) levels, advances O(1) nodes per level.

flashcards.front: Skip list insertion: algorithm?
flashcards.back: Search for insertion position. Randomly determine height h for new node: flip fair coin until tails, h = number of heads. Link node into all levels 0..h-1. Update preceding nodes' forward pointers at each level. Expected O(log n) — same as search.

flashcards.front: Skip list: expected height of tallest node for n elements?
flashcards.back: Each element is promoted to level k with probability (1/2)^k. Expected maximum height = O(log n). With high probability, no node exceeds 2 log n levels. Space: each node expected 2 forward pointers → O(n) total space.

flashcards.front: Skip list vs balanced BST: practical comparison?
flashcards.back: Skip list: simpler to implement, easier to make concurrent (lock-free with CAS), cache-friendly traversal at each level. BST: deterministic height, better worst-case guarantees. Both O(log n) expected/guaranteed. Redis uses skip lists for sorted sets (ZADD/ZRANGE) due to simplicity.

flashcards.front: Skip list space complexity?
flashcards.back: Each element at level 0 (always). At level 1 with probability 1/2. Level k with probability (1/2)^k. Expected pointers per element = Σₖ≥0 (1/2)^k = 2. Total expected space = O(2n) = O(n).

quiz.question: Skip list search for 7 in list [1,3,5,7,9]: how does the search proceed at level 2 if level 2 has nodes [1,5,9]?
options: Start at 1, advance to 5 (5≤7), advance to 9 (9>7), drop to level 1
Start at 1, advance directly to 9 (skip 5), then drop
Start at 9, backtrack to 5
Full scan of level 2
quiz.explanation: At level 2: start at 1. next=5: 5≤7 → advance to 5. next=9: 9>7 → drop one level. At level 1 (or 0), continue from 5. This 'express lane' skips large portions of the list.

quiz.question: Skip list node height determination: coin flip protocol. What is Pr[height ≥ 3]?
quiz.explanation: Height ≥ 3 means: first two flips are heads. Pr[H, H, any] = (1/2)² = 1/4. More precisely: Pr[height ≥ k] = (1/2)^(k-1) since height = 1 + number of heads before first tail.

quiz.question: Why is skip list easier to make concurrent than a balanced BST (like AVL)?
options: Skip list has fewer nodes
Skip list insertion only modifies a few forward pointers — can be done with CAS (compare-and-swap) atomically without locking the whole structure. AVL rotation affects many ancestors simultaneously.
Skip list is sorted
Skip list doesn't require rebalancing
quiz.explanation: Concurrent skip list: insert modifies O(log n) forward pointers independently — each can be updated with CAS. Fine-grained locking or lock-free. AVL rotation: restructures the tree propagating changes up O(log n) levels — harder to atomically coordinate. Java ConcurrentSkipListMap uses this property.

quiz.question: Expected number of nodes examined to search n-element skip list?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(√n)
O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: O(log n) expected. Each level has n/(2^k) elements on average. Search traverses O(log n) levels, O(1) nodes per level. Total O(log n). With high probability bounded by c×log n for any constant c (via Chernoff bounds on geometric random variables).

theory_mcq.question: Each level promotion uses probability 1/2 (coin flip). Why does this specific probability produce EXPECTED O(log n) HEIGHT?
options: Probability 1/2 is arbitrary; any fixed probability gives O(log n) height

GEOMETRIC DISTRIBUTION: the number of levels a node reaches follows a geometric distribution with success probability p=1/2; the EXPECTED number of levels for ONE node is 1/p = 2 (constant); but the MAXIMUM level among n independent nodes is what determines the skip list's HEIGHT; for n nodes each independently promoted with p=1/2, the PROBABILITY that ANY node reaches level k is n*(1/2)^k; setting this to a small constant (union bound) gives k ≈ log2(n); thus the EXPECTED MAXIMUM level (= skip list height) is O(log n); a different fixed probability p would still give O(log n) height (with a different constant factor: log_{1/p}(n)), but p=1/2 is chosen because it gives the LEVEL COUNT vs SPACE OVERHEAD tradeoff: ~2x space overhead vs a balanced BST
Probability 1/2 ensures the skip list always has exactly log2(n) levels
The 1/2 probability is needed because JavaScript's Math.random() returns [0,1)
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Expected height: O(log n) levels due to geometric distribution' and 'Level k: subset of level k-1 elements promoted with probability 1/2' — each level halves the expected number of nodes (n, n/2, n/4, ..., 1), giving log2(n) levels in expectation; p=1/2 specifically balances expected space overhead (2x total pointers) against search speed (log n height).

theory_mcq.question: SEARCH starts at the TOP LEVEL and 'moves right until overshoot, drop down'. Why does starting at the TOP (not the bottom) achieve O(log n) search?
options: Starting at the top is purely a coding convenience with no performance implication

SKIPPING MULTIPLE ELEMENTS PER STEP: the top level has the FEWEST nodes (roughly n/2^(height-1) ≈ O(1) nodes), allowing the search to SKIP LARGE PORTIONS of the list in O(1) steps at this level before needing to drop down; if search started at the BOTTOM (level 0, the complete list), it would need O(n) steps in the worst case — exactly like a regular linked list; by starting HIGH and progressively dropping to denser levels only when needed, the search 'zooms in' on the target — first making big jumps, then smaller jumps, then exact position; this top-down funneling is precisely what gives O(log n) expected search, analogous to binary search's halving
Starting at the top is required to correctly handle the header sentinel node
Top-down search is needed because skip lists don't support bottom-up traversal
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `for(let i=this.level;i>=0;i--)` (decreasing from top level to 0) and 'Search: start at top level, move right until overshoot, drop down' — the top-down funnel strategy: at each level, advance while the next node's key is less than target; when overshooting (next would exceed target), drop one level down; this gives expected O(log n) total work, similar in spirit to binary search.

logic_mcq.question: For a SkipList with inserted keys [3,1,5,2] (in that order), `search(4)` returns `undefined`. Trace why.
options: search(4) traverses levels looking for key=4; since 4 was never inserted, the search correctly fails to find an exact match and returns undefined after `curr.key !== 4` at level 0
search(4) returns undefined because 4 is between existing keys 3 and 5, causing an ambiguous result
The skip list always returns undefined for even numbers due to a hashing quirk
search(4) fails because the skip list wasn't properly rebalanced after 4 inserts
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: search(4)=undefined; keys 1,2,3,5 are in the list but 4 is not; the search correctly navigates to the position where 4 WOULD be (between 3 and 5) but finds curr.key=5≠4 at level 0, so it returns undefined; this is correct behavior — the skip list accurately reports that 4 is not present.

logic_mcq.question: Why are 'skip lists' considered an alternative to BALANCED BSTs (like AVL/Red-Black) for concurrent (multi-threaded) implementations?
options: Skip lists use less memory than balanced BSTs, which matters for concurrency

NO STRUCTURAL REBALANCING: balanced BSTs require ROTATIONS that restructure multiple nodes simultaneously when inserting/deleting — in a concurrent environment, this requires LOCKING multiple nodes (or the whole tree) to maintain consistency during rebalancing, creating contention; skip lists achieve balance PROBABILISTICALLY via coin flips at INSERT time — no subsequent restructuring is ever needed; a skip list insert only modifies LOCAL forward pointers at the levels it participates in, making FINE-GRAINED LOCKING (lock only the nodes being modified) much simpler to implement correctly; this is why skip lists are used in production systems requiring high-concurrency ordered structures (e.g., Redis sorted sets, LevelDB)
Skip lists are faster than BSTs for all operations, making concurrency irrelevant
Balanced BSTs cannot be made concurrent under any circumstances
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Advantages over BST: simpler concurrent implementation, no rotation logic' — rotations in balanced BSTs touch multiple nodes atomically, complicating lock-based concurrency; skip lists avoid rotations entirely (randomization replaces deterministic rebalancing), enabling simpler lock-free or fine-grained locking schemes; this is the primary engineering reason skip lists are chosen in production (Redis ZSET, LevelDB, etc.).

syntax_mcq.question: The `update` array in `insert` tracks `update[i] = curr` for each level i. What PURPOSE does this array serve?
options: update[i] tracks how many times level i has been updated, for statistics

PREDECESSOR TRACKING for INSERTION SPLICING: `update[i]` records the LAST node at level i that is BEFORE the insertion point — this is the node whose `forward[i]` pointer must be updated to point to the new node; since insertion requires SPLICING the new node into POTENTIALLY MULTIPLE LEVELS (from level 0 up to its random newLevel), we need to know, FOR EACH LEVEL, which existing node comes immediately before the insertion point; without tracking these predecessors during the initial top-down search, a second traversal would be needed to find them — `update[]` lets insertion happen in a SINGLE top-down pass
update[i] is used to detect and resolve hash collisions
The array tracks which nodes need to be deleted before insertion
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `const update = new Array(MAX_LEVEL+1).fill(this.header)` populated during the search loop, then used in `update[i].forward[i] = newNode` — update[] captures the predecessor at EACH level during the single top-down search pass, enabling the subsequent splice-in of the new node at all its randomly-determined levels without a second traversal.

lessons.title: Reservoir Sampling
lessons.objective: Implement Algorithm R for reservoir sampling and prove that every element in the stream has equal probability k/n of being in the final sample, regardless of stream length.
concepts: Reservoir sampling: select k items from a stream of unknown size n uniformly
Algorithm R: keep first k items; for item i > k, keep with probability k/i
On keeping item i: replace a random existing reservoir item
Proof: P(item i in reservoir) = k/n for all i
O(n) time, O(k) space
Weighted reservoir sampling: non-uniform weights with same O(n) approach
Applications: uniform random sampling from large datasets, A/B testing assignment
Random sampling node from linked list: equal probability without knowing length
lessons.explanation: Reservoir sampling solves: given a stream of n items (n unknown until end), select k items with uniform probability k/n for each item. Algorithm R: (1) Fill reservoir with first k items. (2) For each subsequent item i (starting at k+1): keep it with probability k/i. If kept, replace a random one of the k reservoir items with item i. Proof by induction that after processing all n items, every item has probability k/n of being in the reservoir. Base case: after first k items, each has probability 1 = k/k. Inductive step: suppose after processing i-1 items, each has probability k/(i-1). When item i arrives: it is kept with probability k/i. Each existing item survives if item i is not kept (prob (i-k)/i) OR item i is kept but the existing item is not the one replaced (prob k/i * (k-1)/k = (k-1)/i). Total survival probability: (i-k)/i + (k-1)/i = (i-1)/i. So each item's new probability: k/(i-1) * (i-1)/i = k/i. After all n items: each has probability k/n.
lessons.analogy: Reservoir sampling is like maintaining a 'best k songs' playlist on a jukebox as new songs stream in. The first k songs always make the playlist. For each new song, you decide to swap it in with a random probability. The probability is calibrated so that after the entire stream, every song has had an equal chance of ending up in the playlist — even though you never knew how many total songs there were.

code_example.explanation: Linked List Random Node (#382, NeetCode 150) is k=1 reservoir sampling. At each node i (1-indexed), keep it with probability 1/i (replace the current result with probability 1/i). After visiting all n nodes, each node has probability 1/n of being the result. This solves the problem without knowing n in advance, using O(1) space.

common_mistakes: Using Math.random() * i < 1 instead of Math.floor(Math.random() * i) === 0 for k=1 sampling — both give probability 1/i but the floor version is more explicit and avoids floating-point subtleties
Not filling the reservoir with the first k items before starting the probabilistic replacement — the first k items should always be included; the random replacement only starts at item k+1

Confusing stream size n with index i in the probability calculation — when processing item i (0-indexed), the replacement probability is k/(i+1) (not k/i), because there are i+1 items seen so far including the current one
lessons.interview_relevance: Linked List Random Node (#382) is NeetCode 150 and directly tests reservoir sampling. Random Pick with Weight (#528) is also NeetCode 150 and tests weighted sampling. The proof that reservoir sampling gives uniform probability (by induction) is specifically evaluated at senior interviews. The O(n) time O(k) space bounds are the expected answer to 'Why is this approach better than storing the full list?'

Then prove by induction for k=1: after processing 3 items, each has probability 1/3. Show the calculation for items 1, 2, and 3.

flashcards.front: Reservoir sampling: formal problem?
flashcards.back: Given a stream of n items (n unknown in advance), select k items uniformly at random (each item has equal probability k/n of selection) using O(k) space and O(n) time with a single pass.

flashcards.front: Reservoir sampling algorithm (k=1, Fisher-Yates variant)?
flashcards.back: Keep the first item. For each subsequent item i (1-indexed starting at 2): replace the current item with probability 1/i. After seeing i items, current item is uniform random among first i items. After all n items: result is uniform among all n.

flashcards.front: Reservoir sampling for k>1: Algorithm R (Vitter)?
flashcards.back: Keep first k items in reservoir. For each subsequent item i (i > k): with probability k/i, replace a RANDOM element in the reservoir. This maintains the invariant: at any point after seeing i items, each item has equal probability k/i of being in the reservoir.

flashcards.front: Reservoir sampling correctness: proof for k=1?
flashcards.back: Induction: after seeing 1 item, it's in reservoir with prob 1/1 ✓. After seeing i items, item j (j≤i) is in reservoir with prob 1/i (by induction). After item i+1: item j stays with prob (1 - 1/(i+1)) × 1/i = i/((i+1)i) = 1/(i+1). New item selected with prob 1/(i+1). All items have equal 1/(i+1) probability ✓.

flashcards.front: Reservoir sampling: what if n is known in advance?
flashcards.back: If n is known: use simple uniform random sampling (random.sample in O(n)). Reservoir sampling's advantage is when n is UNKNOWN (stream). For file/array with known n: choose k random indices in O(k) and read only those elements.

flashcards.front: Weighted reservoir sampling: extension?
flashcards.back: Each item i has weight wᵢ. Probability of selection proportional to weight. Algorithm A-Res: assign each item a key r^(1/wᵢ) where r ~ Uniform(0,1). Keep the k items with the HIGHEST keys. Equivalent to weighted random sampling. O(n log k) with k-element min-heap.

quiz.question: Reservoir sampling k=1: stream=[A,B,C,D,E]. After processing C (3rd item), probability that C is in reservoir?
options: Always 1/3 at this step
quiz.explanation: After processing 3rd item C: with probability 1/3, C replaced reservoir (current item is C). With probability 2/3, didn't replace (current is A or B). By the algorithm: Pr[C in reservoir after 3 items] = 1/3. This generalises: Pr[item i in reservoir after i items] = 1/i.

quiz.question: Reservoir sampling k=3 on stream of 100 items. Probability item 50 is in final reservoir?
quiz.explanation: Reservoir sampling guarantees uniform sampling: each of the n=100 items has probability k/n = 3/100 = 3% of being in the final reservoir of size k=3. This holds for ALL items, including item 50.

quiz.question: After seeing i=10 items with reservoir k=3: item at reservoir position 0. Item 11 arrives. Probability item at position 0 is replaced?
quiz.explanation: Step 1: replace SOME reservoir item with prob 3/11 (k/i = 3/11). Step 2: if replacing, choose which position uniformly: prob 1/3. Pr[position 0 specifically replaced] = 3/11 × 1/3 = 1/11. This ensures item at position 0 stays with prob 10/11 = i/(i+1), maintaining the invariant.

quiz.question: Reservoir sampling requires one pass. What is the space complexity?
options: O(n) — store all items seen
O(k) — only reservoir of size k
O(n log k)
quiz.explanation: Only the reservoir of size k is maintained. No other items are stored. O(k) space regardless of stream length n. This is the key advantage over methods that require storing all items.

theory_mcq.question: Algorithm R keeps element i (i>k) with probability k/i, replacing a RANDOM existing reservoir item. PROVE: why does element i END UP in the final reservoir with probability EXACTLY k/n?
options: Element i has probability k/i of being kept initially, and this probability never changes afterward

TWO-STAGE PROBABILITY: P(item i survives to the end) = P(i is initially SELECTED) × P(i is NEVER REPLACED by later items); P(i selected at step i) = k/i (given); for each SUBSEQUENT item j>i, P(i survives item j's processing) = P(j not selected) + P(j selected but doesn't pick i's slot) = (1-k/j) + (k/j)(1-1/k) = 1-1/j; multiplying survival probabilities for all j from i+1 to n: (1-1/(i+1))(1-1/(i+2))...(1-1/n) = (i/(i+1))(((i+1)/(i+2))...((n-1)/n) — this TELESCOPES to i/n; combining: P(i in final reservoir) = (k/i)×(i/n) = k/n — INDEPENDENT of i, proving uniform probability for ALL elements regardless of position in the stream
The probability k/n only holds for the FIRST k elements; later elements have a different probability
Algorithm R guarantees k/n probability only when n is known in advance
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Proof: P(item i in reservoir) = k/n for all i' — the telescoping product proof is the standard reservoir sampling correctness argument: item i's survival probability through all subsequent steps telescopes from i/n, combined with its initial k/i selection probability, giving exactly k/n; this proof works for ANY position i, confirming uniform sampling regardless of stream order.

theory_mcq.question: Why is reservoir sampling specifically valuable for STREAMING data where n (total stream length) is UNKNOWN in advance?
options: Reservoir sampling requires knowing n in advance; it doesn't work for true streams

SINGLE-PASS, CONSTANT MEMORY: traditional uniform sampling (e.g., generate k random indices from [0,n)) requires KNOWING n upfront; for a stream where n is unknown (e.g., reading a file of unknown size, processing a live data feed), this approach is impossible without first counting all elements (a second pass or extra memory); Algorithm R processes EACH element EXACTLY ONCE in a SINGLE PASS, using ONLY O(k) memory for the reservoir, regardless of how large n eventually turns out to be; this makes it the canonical solution for sampling from data streams, log files of unknown length, or infinite streams
Reservoir sampling is faster than other sampling methods but requires more memory
The technique only works for k=1; larger k requires a different algorithm
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'select k items from a stream of UNKNOWN SIZE n uniformly' and 'O(n) time, O(k) space' — the single-pass, O(k)-space property is exactly what makes reservoir sampling suited for streaming contexts where the total count is unknown until the stream ends (or never ends, for infinite streams); this is the algorithm's defining practical advantage.

logic_mcq.question: LeetCode #382 (Linked List Random Node) uses k=1 reservoir sampling: `if(Math.floor(Math.random()*i)===0) result=curr.val`. Trace why this gives each node EXACTLY 1/n probability.
options: At step i (1-indexed), P(choosing curr) = 1/i; by the telescoping argument with k=1: P(node at position i survives to the end) = (1/i) × (i/n) = 1/n for ALL i, regardless of position in the list — proven by the same telescoping logic as general reservoir sampling
Each node has probability 1/i only, which decreases for later nodes, making early nodes more likely to be selected
The probability is always 1/2 since Math.random() returns values in [0,1)
P(selection) = 1/n only for the LAST node; earlier nodes have higher probability
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's comment: 'This is k=1 reservoir sampling: keep current with prob 1/i; After n items: P(each item) = 1/n' — applying the general k/n proof with k=1: P(node i survives)=(1/i)×(i/n)=1/n; this confirms EVERY node, regardless of its position in the linked list, has exactly equal 1/n probability of being the final selected result.

logic_mcq.question: `verifyUniformity` checks that 'max deviation should be << expected'. For streamSize=100, k=10, trials=10000, what does a SMALL max deviation CONFIRM about the implementation?
options: A small deviation confirms the implementation has no bugs in array indexing

STATISTICAL VALIDATION OF UNIFORMITY: expected count per element = k/streamSize*trials = 10/100*10000 = 1000; if the implementation correctly samples UNIFORMLY (each element equally likely to be selected), the OBSERVED counts across 10000 independent trials should CLUSTER TIGHTLY around 1000 (by the law of large numbers and central limit theorem, fluctuations should be proportional to sqrt(expected count) ≈ sqrt(1000) ≈ 32, not hundreds); a small max deviation (say, under 100, i.e., 10% of expected) empirically CONFIRMS the k/n uniform probability proof holds in practice, providing experimental validation alongside the theoretical proof
Small deviation indicates the random number generator has high entropy
Max deviation measures the time complexity of the algorithm, not correctness
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: 'Each element should appear in about k/streamSize * trials = 1000 samples' and 'Max deviation should be << expected (e.g., < 100 = 10%)' — this is empirical verification of the theoretical k/n uniformity proof; statistical fluctuation theory predicts deviations on the order of sqrt(expected count); a small max deviation provides experimental confidence that the implementation correctly achieves uniform sampling, not just that the theoretical proof is sound.

syntax_mcq.question: In `reservoirSample`, the replacement check is `const j = Math.floor(Math.random()*(i+1)); if(j<k) reservoir[j]=stream[i];`. Why `(i+1)` and not `(i)`?
options: i+1 is used to avoid a potential index-out-of-bounds error

0-INDEXED ELEMENT COUNTING: at array index i (0-indexed), this is the (i+1)-th element in the stream (1-indexed count); the algorithm needs P(keep element)=k/(i+1) since 'i+1' is the TRUE COUNT of elements seen so far (including the current one); `Math.random()*(i+1)` generates a uniform integer in [0, i+1) — i.e., i+1 EQUALLY LIKELY outcomes; the condition `j<k` then correctly gives probability k/(i+1) of replacement, matching the algorithm's required k/i formula (using 1-indexed i in the math, which corresponds to (i+1) in 0-indexed code)
i+1 converts the array length to its 0-indexed equivalent
The +1 compensates for the k items already filled in the reservoir
syntax_mcq.explanation: The lesson's math uses 1-indexed position i (so element i has probability k/i of being kept), but the JavaScript array is 0-indexed; at 0-indexed array position `i`, we've seen `i+1` total elements (1-indexed count); `Math.random()*(i+1)` correctly generates the range needed for probability k/(i+1), matching the 1-indexed formula k/i when accounting for the index shift.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo Methods
lessons.objective: Implement Monte Carlo estimation for Pi and understand the error bound, confidence intervals, and when Monte Carlo methods are preferred over exact algorithms.
concepts: Monte Carlo: use random sampling to estimate a quantity
Convergence: error decreases as O(1/sqrt(n)) with n samples
Pi estimation: ratio of points inside unit circle to total random points
Confidence interval: 95% CI = estimate ± 1.96 * std/sqrt(n)
When to use Monte Carlo: exact algorithm is intractable or complex
Monte Carlo integration: estimate integrals in high dimensions
Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo: Las Vegas always correct, Monte Carlo may have error
Miller-Rabin primality: probabilistic test, O(k log n) time, error rate 4^(-k)
lessons.explanation: Monte Carlo methods use random sampling to estimate quantities that are difficult to compute exactly. The simplest example: estimate Pi by sampling uniformly in the unit square [0,1] x [0,1]. A point (x,y) is inside the unit circle if x² + y² <= 1. The fraction of points inside the circle approximates Pi/4, so Pi ≈ 4 * (points inside / total points). The error decreases as O(1/sqrt(n)) by the Central Limit Theorem: with n samples, the standard deviation of the estimate is sigma/sqrt(n) where sigma is the standard deviation of a single sample. For Pi estimation, sigma ≈ 0.524, so the 95% confidence interval width is 2 * 1.96 * 0.524/sqrt(n) ≈ 2.05/sqrt(n). To get Pi accurate to 4 decimal places (error < 0.0001), you need n ≈ (2.05/0.0001)² ≈ 4 * 10^8 samples — Monte Carlo is inefficient for high precision but excellent for quick approximations or high-dimensional problems where exact integration is infeasible. Miller-Rabin primality test: probabilistically determines if n is prime. Each round reduces false-positive probability from composite-looking-prime to at most 1/4. With k rounds, error rate is 4^(-k).
lessons.analogy: Monte Carlo Pi estimation is like estimating the area of a lake by randomly dropping pebbles from a helicopter over a known square region. The fraction that lands in the lake estimates the lake's fraction of the total area. More pebbles means a better estimate, but you always need sqrt(n) times more pebbles to halve the error — it is fundamentally less efficient than surveying the boundary exactly.

code_example.explanation: Miller-Rabin uses modular exponentiation with BigInt for large numbers. The test is based on Fermat's little theorem and Miller-Rabin witnesses. A composite number passes the test (appears prime) for a random witness with probability at most 1/4. With k=10 independent rounds, the false positive probability is at most 4^(-10) ≈ 10^(-6). Used in practice for cryptographic key generation.

common_mistakes: Thinking Monte Carlo error decreases faster than O(1/sqrt(n)) — the Central Limit Theorem gives O(1/sqrt(n)) convergence for i.i.d. samples; no amount of clever sampling changes this fundamental rate for standard Monte Carlo

Confusing Monte Carlo correctness with Las Vegas correctness — Monte Carlo algorithms (Miller-Rabin, Bloom filter) can give wrong answers; Las Vegas algorithms (Quicksort, Quickselect) always give correct answers, with randomness only affecting speed
Not using BigInt for Miller-Rabin modular exponentiation with large n — JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53; always use BigInt for modular arithmetic with n > 10^15
lessons.interview_relevance: Monte Carlo methods appear in system design interviews for streaming analytics (estimating cardinality with HyperLogLog), probabilistic data structures (Bloom filters, Count-Min Sketch), and interview questions about estimating quantities from samples. Miller-Rabin appears in cryptography-adjacent interviews. The key insight: O(1/sqrt(n)) convergence rate and the Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo distinction.

Then implement Miller-Rabin and verify it correctly identifies 100 prime numbers from a known list. flashcards.front: Monte Carlo method: general framework?
flashcards.back: Estimate a quantity by RANDOM SAMPLING. Generate random samples, check if they satisfy a condition, use fraction to estimate probability/area/value. Result improves with more samples. Error decreases as O(1/√N) where N = samples (Central Limit Theorem).

flashcards.front: Monte Carlo for π estimation: approach?
flashcards.back: Sample random points (x,y) ∈ [0,1]². Count how many fall inside the unit circle (x²+y²≤1). Fraction inside circle × 4 ≈ π. With N samples: error ≈ 2/√N. For π accurate to 4 decimal places: N ≈ 10^8 samples needed (slow).

flashcards.front: Monte Carlo integration: general formula?
flashcards.back: Estimate ∫f(x)dx over [a,b]: sample N uniform points xᵢ ∈ [a,b], compute mean of f(xᵢ). Estimate = (b-a) × (1/N)Σf(xᵢ). Standard error = (b-a)×std(f)/√N. Works in any dimension — unlike quadrature methods which suffer the curse of dimensionality.

flashcards.front: Primality testing: Miller-Rabin (Monte Carlo)?
flashcards.back: For prime p, for any base a: a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Miller-Rabin tests k random bases. If any base witnesses COMPOSITENESS: definitely composite. If all k bases pass: probably prime (probability of false positive ≤ 4^(-k)). O(k log² n) per test. For k=40: probability of error < 10^(-24).

flashcards.front: Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo recap: correctness guarantees?
flashcards.back: LAS VEGAS: ALWAYS CORRECT, random runtime. Can bound expected runtime but not guarantee it for every run. MONTE CARLO: ALWAYS TERMINATES, may be WRONG with small probability. Can bound error probability but cannot guarantee correctness for every run. Both are randomised algorithms with different guarantees.

flashcards.front: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS): used in AI?
flashcards.back: Game-tree search combining Monte Carlo simulation with UCB (Upper Confidence Bound). Selects promising moves, plays random games to completion (rollout), backpropagates win/loss rates. Used in AlphaGo (combined with deep learning). O(n) simulations per move, improves with more computation time.

quiz.question: Monte Carlo π estimation: 10,000 samples give π̂=3.14. Expected error magnitude?

High dimensions increase accuracy

theory_mcq.question: Monte Carlo Pi estimation has error that decreases as O(1/√n). What does this convergence rate imply about the COST of improving precision?
options: Doubling n halves the error, giving efficient linear improvement

DIMINISHING RETURNS: to REDUCE the error by a factor of 10 (one more decimal digit of precision), n must INCREASE by a factor of 100 (since error ∝ 1/√n means to make error 10x smaller, n must be 10²=100x larger); this is SLOWER than many other numerical methods (e.g., trapezoidal integration converges as O(1/n) or O(1/n²) for smooth functions); the O(1/√n) rate is a FUNDAMENTAL LIMITATION of Monte Carlo methods, NOT a particular implementation flaw — it follows from the Central Limit Theorem applied to the sample mean's standard error; Monte Carlo's value isn't fast convergence but rather APPLICABILITY to high-dimensional or analytically intractable problems where other methods fail entirely
The error decreases exponentially, making n=1000 sufficient for any practical precision
O(1/sqrt(n)) error means precision is independent of the number of samples
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Convergence: error decreases as O(1/sqrt(n)) with n samples' — this slow convergence (compared to deterministic numerical methods) is a known tradeoff; Monte Carlo's true advantage emerges in HIGH-DIMENSIONAL problems where deterministic grid-based methods suffer from the 'curse of dimensionality' (exponential cost in dimension), while Monte Carlo's O(1/sqrt(n)) convergence is DIMENSION-INDEPENDENT.

theory_mcq.question: Miller-Rabin has 'error rate 4^(-k)' for k rounds. Why does running MULTIPLE INDEPENDENT rounds REDUCE the error EXPONENTIALLY (not just linearly)?
options: Multiple rounds reduce error linearly, not exponentially; the 4^(-k) formula is incorrect

INDEPENDENT TRIAL MULTIPLICATION: each round of Miller-Rabin independently tests a RANDOM witness `a`; for a COMPOSITE number, AT MOST 1/4 of possible witnesses FAIL to detect compositeness (this is a number-theoretic guarantee, not assumed); running k INDEPENDENT rounds means the algorithm fails to detect compositeness ONLY IF ALL k rounds happen to pick a 'bad' witness; since each round's witness choice is INDEPENDENT, P(all k rounds fail) = P(round fails)^k ≤ (1/4)^k = 4^(-k); this EXPONENTIAL decrease (not linear, like 1/(4k)) is the power of independent probabilistic trials — for k=10, error ≤ 4^(-10) ≈ 10^(-6), an extremely small and PRACTICALLY NEGLIGIBLE probability
The error rate decreases exponentially only for numbers larger than 10^9
4^(-k) represents the error BEFORE any rounds are run; it decreases linearly afterward
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Miller-Rabin primality: probabilistic test, O(k log n) time, error rate 4^(-k)' — the multiplicative independence of trial outcomes is the source of exponential error reduction; this is the same principle behind amplification in randomized algorithms generally: running k independent trials of an algorithm with constant error probability p reduces overall error to p^k, exponentially small in k.

logic_mcq.question: For `estimatePi(1000000)`, the result is approximately 3.1416 with small error. Explain the GEOMETRIC PRINCIPLE behind this estimation.
options: Random (x,y) points in [0,1]×[0,1] (unit square, area=1); points satisfying x²+y²≤1 fall within the QUARTER UNIT CIRCLE (area=π/4); the RATIO of points inside the circle to total points approximates the AREA RATIO π/4 ÷ 1 = π/4; multiplying by 4 recovers π — confirmed by direct execution showing convergence near 3.14159
The points are generated on a circle, and pi is computed from the circumference formula
Pi is computed by counting the number of random points that land exactly on the circle boundary
The estimation uses the law of cosines applied to random triangle vertices
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: estimatePi(1000000)≈3.1432 (error≈0.0017, consistent with O(1/sqrt(n)) convergence for n=10^6); the geometric principle: random points uniformly in the unit square [0,1]² have probability π/4 of falling inside the quarter circle x²+y²≤1; counting the fraction inside and multiplying by 4 estimates π.

logic_mcq.question: Why is `millerRabin` classified as MONTE CARLO rather than LAS VEGAS, despite its high accuracy?
options: Miller-Rabin has a SMALL but NONZERO probability of FALSE POSITIVE (declaring a composite number 'probably prime') — this matches the Monte Carlo definition exactly: 'may be incorrect with bounded probability'; in contrast, a LAS VEGAS algorithm is ALWAYS correct (possibly taking variable time); Miller-Rabin can NEVER be Las Vegas because its correctness guarantee is fundamentally PROBABILISTIC (bounded by 4^(-k), never zero for finite k); this is distinct from quicksort/quickselect (Las Vegas), which ALWAYS produce the correct sorted/selected result, just with VARIABLE (randomized) running time
Miller-Rabin is Monte Carlo because it uses random number generation, regardless of correctness guarantees
Miller-Rabin would be Las Vegas if k were increased to infinity
The classification depends on the size of n being tested, not the algorithm's structure
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo: Las Vegas always correct, Monte Carlo may have error' and 'Miller-Rabin primality: probabilistic test...error rate 4^(-k)' — the defining distinction is WHAT varies: Las Vegas algorithms have variable RUNTIME but guaranteed CORRECTNESS; Monte Carlo algorithms have FIXED runtime (or bounded) but variable CORRECTNESS; Miller-Rabin's nonzero (though tiny) error probability places it firmly in the Monte Carlo category.

syntax_mcq.question: `millerRabin` uses `BigInt` for `modPow`. Why is BigInt NECESSARY here rather than regular JavaScript numbers?
options: BigInt is used purely for code style; regular numbers would work identically

PRECISION OVERFLOW PREVENTION: JavaScript's regular Number type uses IEEE 754 double-precision floating point, which can EXACTLY represent integers only up to 2^53 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER); `modPow` computes `base*base % mod` REPEATEDLY — for n near 10^9 (as in the test `millerRabin(982451653)`), intermediate values like base*base can reach ~10^18, FAR EXCEEDING 2^53≈9×10^15; without BigInt, this multiplication would lose precision (silently producing WRONG results due to floating-point rounding), corrupting the modular exponentiation; BigInt provides ARBITRARY PRECISION integer arithmetic, ensuring exact computation regardless of n's magnitude
BigInt is required because JavaScript doesn't support the modulo operator for regular numbers
BigInt is used to enable parallel computation of multiple modPow calls
syntax_mcq.explanation: For n=982451653 (~10^9), intermediate squaring in modPow can produce values up to n²≈10^18, which exceeds JavaScript's safe integer range (2^53≈9×10^15); using regular Number arithmetic here would silently corrupt results via floating-point imprecision; BigInt's arbitrary-precision integers ensure the modular exponentiation remains exact, which is essential for Miller-Rabin's correctness on numbers in this range.

lessons.title: Hashing With Probability Guarantees
lessons.objective: Explain universal hashing, consistent hashing, and polynomial hashing, and quantify the collision probability that makes these hash functions suitable for security-sensitive applications.
concepts: Universal hashing: family of hash functions where P(collision) <= 1/m for any two keys
Definition: for any x != y, |{h in H: h(x) = h(y)}| <= |H|/m
Carter-Wegman universal family: h_{a,b}(x) = ((ax+b) mod p) mod m
Perfect hashing: zero collisions in O(n) space using two-level hashing
Birthday paradox: expected first collision after O(sqrt(m)) insertions
Polynomial hashing: Rabin fingerprint, Rabin-Karp rolling hash
Expected collisions with universal hashing: E[collisions] = n(n-1)/(2m)
Security: hash DoS attacks exploited fixed hash seeds; use random seeds
lessons.explanation: Universal hashing provides formal collision probability guarantees. A family H of hash functions is universal if for any two distinct keys x and y, the probability over randomly chosen h in H that h(x) = h(y) is at most 1/m (where m is the table size). This means that for any input (even adversarially chosen), the expected number of collisions is at most n/m — the same as a random hash. The Carter-Wegman family: h_{a,b}(x) = ((ax+b) mod p) mod m, where p is a prime larger than the universe size, and a (a != 0) and b are chosen randomly from [0, p-1]. This family is universal. Perfect hashing: uses two-level hashing. First level: hash n keys to n buckets using a universal hash. For each bucket with k_i keys, use a secondary hash table of size k_i² with a different universal hash (expected collisions < 1). Total space: O(n). Birthday paradox: in a hash table of size m, the expected number of insertions before the first collision is O(sqrt(m)). This explains why hash tables need load factor < 1 to avoid frequent collisions. Hash DoS: if a hash function is deterministic (fixed), an attacker can craft many inputs with the same hash, creating O(n) collision chains. Random seed selection (as in Python's dict since 3.3 and Java's HashMap in recent versions) prevents this.
lessons.analogy: Universal hashing is like randomly assigning mailmen to routes. If the assignment is truly random (universal), no matter how many letters are addressed to the same block (adversarial input), the expected imbalance in any mailman's load is bounded. An attacker who knows the route assignment can exploit a fixed assignment but cannot predict a random one.

code_example.explanation: The two-level perfect hash uses O(n) total space because the expected total size of all second-level tables is O(n). For bucket i with k_i keys, the second-level table has k_i² slots. The expected total: E[sum k_i²] = O(n) because a universal hash distributes n keys into n buckets with expected k_i=1 and Var[k_i]=O(1/n). The expected sum of squares is O(n).

common_mistakes: Using a deterministic hash function without a random seed in security-sensitive applications — deterministic hashes can be reverse-engineered or attacked with specially crafted inputs; always use a random seed

Confusing universal hashing guarantee (1/m for any two fixed keys) with uniformity (P(key maps to slot j) = 1/m) — universal hashing bounds pairwise collision probability; uniformity bounds single-key distribution; both are needed for a good hash table

Not accounting for the birthday paradox when choosing table size — for a table of size m, first collision expected after O(sqrt(m)) insertions; for 99.9% collision-free performance, use m > n²/2 (perfect hashing) or load factor < 0.7 (chaining)
lessons.interview_relevance: Universal hashing appears in theoretical interviews at companies with strong algorithms focus (Jane Street, Hudson River Trading, competitive programming-style interviews). The practical application — hash DoS attacks and the Python/Java response of randomised hash seeds — appears in security-focused system design interviews. The birthday paradox and expected collisions are specifically tested.

flashcards.front: Universal hashing: what is it?
flashcards.back: A FAMILY of hash functions where for any two distinct keys x and y, the probability (over random choice of hash function from the family) that h(x) = h(y) ≤ 1/m. This guarantees O(1) expected per operation in a hash table regardless of input — even adversarial input.

flashcards.front: Universal hashing: simple construction for integer keys?
flashcards.back: For keys in [0, p-1] (p prime): h_{a,b}(x) = ((ax + b) mod p) mod m. Choose a,b uniformly at random from [1,p-1] and [0,p-1]. This family is 2-universal: Pr[h(x)=h(y)] ≤ 1/m for any x≠y. O(1) per hash computation.

flashcards.front: Perfect hashing: what does it achieve?
flashcards.back: O(1) WORST CASE lookup for a STATIC set of n keys. Build: O(n) expected. Two-level scheme: outer hash partitions keys into groups, inner hash (unique for each group) is perfect within each group. Achieves O(n) total space and O(1) worst case lookup — no collisions at all.

flashcards.front: Fingerprinting / polynomial hashing: how it detects string equality?
flashcards.back: Represent string S as a polynomial: P_S(x) = Σ S[i]×x^i (mod p). For random x: Pr[P_S(x) = P_T(x)] ≤ |S|/p if S≠T (Schwartz-Zippel). Choose large prime p, random x → fingerprint. Two strings with equal fingerprints are almost certainly equal.

flashcards.front: Count-Min Sketch: what is it?
flashcards.back: Approximate frequency counting for data streams. d hash functions × w counters each. Add item x: increment counter[i][h_i(x)] for each i. Query frequency of x: min(counter[i][h_i(x)]) over all i. Overestimates true frequency by at most ε×N with probability 1-δ where d=log(1/δ), w=e/ε.

flashcards.front: HyperLogLog: what does it estimate?
flashcards.back: CARDINALITY of a multiset (count distinct elements) using O(log log n) bits per hash function. Hashes each element to a bit string; tracks the maximum number of leading zeros seen. Expected estimate error ≈ 1.04/√(2^b) where b bits of precision. Used in Redis, Flink, BigQuery.

n²/m
quiz.explanation: For key x: expected collisions = Σ_{y≠x} Pr[h(x)=h(y)] ≤ (n-1)/m ≤ n/n = 1. With universal hashing, each key has at most 1 expected collision regardless of adversarial key choice. This guarantees O(1) expected lookup even with adversarial input.

quiz.question: Count-Min Sketch: item 'apple' has true frequency 100 in a stream of 10000 items. Sketch with d=3, w=1000. Estimated frequency?

≥100 — Count-Min always OVERESTIMATES (never underestimates)

100 ± 10 (symmetric error)
quiz.explanation: Count-Min Sketch OVERESTIMATES: counters are incremented by ALL items that hash to the same bucket (not just 'apple'). The minimum over d hash functions gives the tightest upper bound. Estimate ≥ true frequency always. Error bounded: estimate ≤ true_freq + ε×N with probability 1-δ.

quiz.question: Schwartz-Zippel lemma: two distinct n-character strings S≠T. Pr[hash(S)=hash(T)] with polynomial hash over prime p?
options: n/p
quiz.explanation: Polynomial hash: P_S(x) = Σ S[i]×x^i mod p. P_S - P_T is a nonzero polynomial of degree ≤ n-1. By Schwartz-Zippel: Pr[P_S(x) = P_T(x)] = Pr[(P_S-P_T)(x)=0] ≤ (n-1)/p ≤ n/p for random x. Choose p > n/ε → collision probability < ε.

theory_mcq.question: Universal hashing guarantees `P(collision) <= 1/m` for ANY two DISTINCT keys, NOT for a specific adversarial pair. Why does this property defeat HASH-FLOODING ATTACKS that fixed hash functions are vulnerable to?
options: Universal hashing makes collisions completely impossible, eliminating the attack vector entirely

ATTACKER CANNOT PRECOMPUTE COLLISIONS: with a FIXED, KNOWN hash function, an attacker can PRECOMPUTE a large set of keys that ALL collide (mapping to the same bucket), then submit these keys to overload a single bucket (causing O(n) operations instead of O(1)) — this is the classic 'hash flooding' DoS attack; with UNIVERSAL HASHING, the hash function's PARAMETERS (a, b in Carter-Wegman) are chosen RANDOMLY at RUNTIME, UNKNOWN to the attacker in advance; the attacker CANNOT precompute a colliding key set because they don't know which specific hash function will be used; even if they craft keys that collide under ONE random instance, those same keys are UNLIKELY to collide under a DIFFERENT random instance (P<=1/m for any fixed pair, but the attacker can't target a fixed pair without knowing a,b)
Universal hashing is faster than fixed hashing, leaving attackers no time to exploit collisions
The attack is defeated because universal hash functions always use SHA-256 internally
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Security: hash DoS attacks exploited fixed hash seeds; use random seeds' — the security property comes from RANDOMIZING the hash function choice at runtime (unknown to attackers), not from making collisions impossible; this is precisely why production languages (Python, Ruby, Perl) introduced randomized hash seeding after hash-flooding attacks were discovered around 2011-2012.

theory_mcq.question: PERFECT HASHING uses 'second-level hash tables of size k_i^2' (squared bucket size) to GUARANTEE zero collisions. Why does squaring the size make collision-free hashing ACHIEVABLE?
options: Squaring is required because hash functions inherently need quadratic space

BIRTHDAY PARADOX THRESHOLD: for a bucket with k_i keys, using a universal hash into a table of size k_i² makes EXPECTED COLLISIONS E[collisions] = k_i*(k_i-1)/(2*k_i²) < 1/2 (using the universal hashing collision bound); since EXPECTED collisions is LESS THAN 1, by a Markov-inequality-style argument, the PROBABILITY of ZERO collisions is AT LEAST 1/2 for ANY random hash function chosen from the universal family; this means RETRYING with a fresh random hash function (the `do...while(collision)` loop in the code) succeeds in EXPECTED O(1) attempts, guaranteeing eventual collision-free placement; this squaring trick is the core insight of FKS (Fredman-Komlós-Szemerédi) perfect hashing
k_i² ensures the table has enough memory to store all keys without any hashing at all
Squaring the bucket size doubles the hash function's output range, eliminating collisions by definition
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code comment: 'Second level: for each bucket of size k_i, use hash table of size k_i^2' and 'retry until no collision' — the squared size ensures E[collisions]<1/2 via the universal hashing bound, making P(zero collisions)≥1/2; the retry loop (`do...while(collision)`) then succeeds in EXPECTED 2 attempts, achieving guaranteed O(1) worst-case lookup with O(n) total expected space (since Σk_i²=O(n) in expectation for the first-level hash).

logic_mcq.question: For `testUniversality(100, 100000)`, the observed collision rate is approximately 0.0106 versus expected `1/m=0.01`. Is this consistent with the universal hashing GUARANTEE?
options: Yes — the universal hashing property states P(collision)<=1/m; the observed rate 0.0106 is close to but the guarantee is an UPPER BOUND, and statistical fluctuation over 100000 trials easily explains a small deviation from the theoretical 0.01; this is CONSISTENT with (not a violation of) the universal hashing property
No — 0.0106 exceeds 0.01, proving the hash family violates the universal hashing guarantee
The test is inconclusive because m=100 is too small a table size
The discrepancy indicates a bug in the UniversalHash implementation that must be fixed
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: observed collision rate ≈ 0.0106 for m=100 (expected 1/m=0.01); the universal hashing bound P(collision)<=1/m is a GUARANTEE on the EXACT probability over the random choice of hash function from the family — for Carter-Wegman hashing, the bound is actually achieved with equality for prime p and uniform random a,b; small deviations (1.06% vs 1.00%) across 100,000 trials are explained by standard statistical sampling variance, not a violation.

logic_mcq.question: The Carter-Wegman hash `h(x) = ((ax+b) mod p) mod m` requires `p` to be a LARGE PRIME GREATER than the universe size. Why is PRIMALITY of p specifically required (not just any large number)?
options: Primality is a stylistic convention; any large number works equally well

MODULAR ARITHMETIC PROPERTIES: the universal hashing PROOF relies on properties of the MULTIPLICATIVE GROUP modulo p; when p is PRIME, the residues {1, 2, ..., p-1} form a FIELD under multiplication (every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse) — this algebraic structure is ESSENTIAL for proving that for ANY two distinct keys x≠y, the equation `(ax+b) mod p = (ay+b) mod p` has EXACTLY ONE solution for `a` (given any b) among the p-1 possible non-zero values; if p were COMPOSITE, this uniqueness property could FAIL (zero divisors could create MULTIPLE solutions), breaking the formal universal hashing guarantee P(collision)<=1/m
Primality ensures the hash function runs faster due to CPU optimizations for prime moduli
p must be prime only to satisfy JavaScript's numeric overflow constraints
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Carter-Wegman universal family: h_{a,b}(x) = ((ax+b) mod p) mod m' — the formal universal hashing proof requires p prime specifically because modular arithmetic mod a prime forms a field (Z/pZ), where the equation ax≡ay (mod p) for x≠y has a unique solution for a (namely a≡0, excluded since a is chosen non-zero); this field structure is the foundation of the universal hashing collision bound proof.

syntax_mcq.question: `UniversalHash` constructor picks `this.a = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random()*(p-1))`, ensuring `a` is in `[1, p-1]` (never 0). Why must `a` be NON-ZERO?
options: a=0 would cause a division-by-zero error in the hash computation

DEGENERATE HASH FUNCTION: if a=0, the hash formula becomes `h(x) = ((0*x+b) mod p) mod m = b mod m` — a CONSTANT, independent of x; EVERY key would hash to the SAME bucket (b mod m), making `P(collision)=1` for ALL key pairs (complete failure of the universal hashing guarantee P<=1/m); excluding a=0 is ESSENTIAL because it's the only value that destroys the hash function's dependence on the INPUT — all other a values in [1,p-1] still vary the output based on x, preserving the universal property
a=0 would make the hash function take O(n) time instead of O(1)
JavaScript's modulo operator returns NaN when the dividend includes a zero coefficient
syntax_mcq.explanation: The exclusion of a=0 is mathematically critical: with a=0, h(x)=b mod m for ALL x (a constant function), which trivially has P(collision)=1 for any two distinct keys — completely violating the universal hashing guarantee; the constructor's `1 + Math.floor(Math.random()*(p-1))` correctly generates a in [1, p-1], excluding the degenerate a=0 case.

lessons.title: Probabilistic Algorithm Thinking
lessons.objective: Classify any algorithm as deterministic, Las Vegas, or Monte Carlo, select the appropriate probabilistic technique for any randomness-related problem, and map all Module 9 NeetCode 150 problems.
concepts: Three categories: Deterministic, Las Vegas, Monte Carlo
Deterministic: always same output for same input, no randomness
Las Vegas: always correct, expected efficient (Quicksort, skip lists, reservoir sampling)
Monte Carlo: may be incorrect with bounded probability (Miller-Rabin, Bloom filter)
When randomisation helps: breaking adversarial patterns, space reduction, streaming
When not to randomise: when correctness is critical and exact algorithms exist
Module 9 NeetCode 150 problems mapped
Probability toolkit: expected value, indicator variables, Markov/Chebyshev bounds
lessons.explanation: Probabilistic algorithms solve problems that are difficult, slow, or impossible to solve deterministically with the same efficiency. The three-category classification: Deterministic algorithms have no randomness and always give the same output. Las Vegas algorithms use randomness and always give the correct output but may vary in runtime (Quicksort, skip list, reservoir sampling). Monte Carlo algorithms use randomness and give correct output with high probability, but may give incorrect output with a small bounded probability (Miller-Rabin primality, Bloom filter false positives, Monte Carlo integration with error bars). When randomisation helps: (1) Avoiding adversarial input (randomised QuickSort vs sorted input attack). (2) Streaming algorithms where O(n) space is too much (reservoir sampling in O(k) space). (3) Probabilistic data structures where exact answers cost too much space (Bloom filter vs full set). (4) Parallel/distributed algorithms where coordination is expensive (randomised leader election). The probability toolkit: expected value via linearity (E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even if dependent), indicator random variables, Markov inequality (P(X >= a) <= E[X]/a), and Chebyshev inequality for variance-based bounds.
lessons.analogy: Probabilistic algorithm selection is like choosing a risk strategy in engineering. Deterministic algorithms are like a bridge designed to handle all possible loads exactly (expensive but guaranteed). Las Vegas algorithms are like a bridge designed correctly but built slightly differently each time (always safe, cost varies). Monte Carlo algorithms are like weather forecasting (gives the best estimate with quantified uncertainty, sometimes wrong). The choice depends on the cost of being wrong.

code_example.explanation: Random Pick with Weight uses prefix sums + binary search. The prefix array converts weights to cumulative probabilities. A uniform random float in [0, total] selects each index proportionally to its weight. Binary search finds the correct index in O(log n). This is the foundation for weighted sampling, used in tree node probability selection (Module 3) and random test case generation.

common_mistakes: Classifying reservoir sampling as Monte Carlo — reservoir sampling always returns a correct uniform sample; it is Las Vegas, not Monte Carlo; Monte Carlo algorithms can give wrong answers, reservoir sampling cannot

Using a hash set instead of reservoir sampling for large-stream random sampling — storing all stream elements in a Set to pick from at the end requires O(n) space; reservoir sampling requires only O(k) space

Not considering Las Vegas algorithms when randomness could help but exact correctness is required — Las Vegas algorithms combine the best of both: randomness for efficiency, determinism for correctness guarantee
lessons.interview_relevance: Module 9 covers 3 NeetCode 150 problems: Linked List Random Node (#382, reservoir sampling k=1), Random Pick with Weight (#528, prefix sum + binary search), and Shuffle an Array (#384, Fisher-Yates). All three test specific probabilistic algorithm knowledge. The three-category classification (Deterministic / Las Vegas / Monte Carlo) is the conceptual framework that allows explaining any randomised algorithm's correctness properties.
